💰🇲🇽 <u>SHEINBAUM MOVES TO CAP EVERY PUBLIC PENSION AT THE PRESIDENT'S SALARY</u>

Ending the plush pensions of ex-officials has already saved nearly 5 billion pesos — some were collecting up to a million pesos a month. Now Sheinbaum will send a reform to lock the cap into law: no public pension above the president's paycheck. Republican austerity that starts at the top, not the bottom.

🇲🇽🏭 <u>MEXICO IS NOW THE WORLD'S #2 EXPORTER OF AI INPUTS — ONLY CHINA IS AHEAD</u>

Mexico consolidated itself as the second-largest exporter of the products used to build artificial intelligence systems, behind only China, the World Bank reported. Nearly half of global AI-input exports now come from developing economies — China, Mexico, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand — powered by semiconductors, electronics and data-center equipment. The country they insisted was just a maquila is now wiring the AI boom.

🔥🇲🇽 "Golden pensions no longer exist in our country." "Golden pensions no longer exist in our country — nobody collects a million pesos a month anymore, sometimes for posts they held for two, three, four months." — Luisa María Alcalde, Presidential Legal Counsel Answering questions on the transparency decree: no public servant in Mexico can earn more than the president. The multimillion-peso lifetime pensions for short stints in office — a fixture of the old regime — are gone.

🔥🇲🇽 "This space has the right of reply. What they don't want is for the government to reply to the media." "What I'm saying here will surely be commented on all day — it's a reply to what they've been putting out from the media, from social networks. This space has the right of reply. What they don't want is for the government to be able to reply to the media." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, answering the censorship charges Asked directly: can outlets be fined for content? "No." Can they be censored? "No." The guidelines say three things: publish your ethics code, name your audience ombudsman, set up a complaint channel. Article 6 of the Constitution guarantees the right of reply — to everyone.
banner: "THIS SPACE HAS THE RIGHT TO REPLY"

text: 📺🇲🇽 The "censorship" rule in full: paid segments get a "P" on screen. That's it. "A small 'P' — a plaque with the letter 'P', for 'publicidad' — appears at the start and end of a paid segment. That is all... What does that have to do with censorship?" — Luisa María Alcalde, Presidential Legal Counsel The guidelines let audiences tell ads from news and opinion from information: a "P" plaque on TV, a prior verbal notice on radio, a banner at the start and end of opinion shows. Print has done it for decades — "paid insertion." Pundits spent a week claiming hosts would have to stop every ten seconds.
banner: ADS GET A 'P' LABEL — THAT'S IT

text: 📺🇲🇽 "The State will not decide what is true. The media will — through their own codes of ethics." "The State will not evaluate what is true and what is not. Media outlets themselves, through their Codes of Ethics, will establish how they guarantee truthful information." — Luisa María Alcalde, Presidential Legal Counsel For a week, columnists called the new broadcast guidelines — still in public consultation — "censorship." Alcalde walked through them line by line: outlets write their own ethics codes, name their own audience ombudsman, run their own complaint process. The regulator only acts if an outlet skips those steps — never over content.

🔥🇲🇽 Every federal contract, published monthly. Pemex and CFE subsidiaries open their books. "Right now it's published every three months. We're going to publish monthly — every contract of the Federal Government will be published every month." — Raquel Buenrostro, Anticorruption Secretary The decree hits four areas: public contracting, Pemex/CFE subsidiaries (financial statements, corporate governance, reports filed with foreign agencies), audits, and an open invitation to all branches and levels of government. The 17 old reserve categories collapse into two: public interest and national security.

🇲🇽⚖️ "It is total transparency of the Government of Mexico." "With this Decree we no longer leave it 'to the criterion of the public servant'... It is total transparency of the Government of Mexico." — President Claudia Sheinbaum, signing the transparency decree Signed this morning: no official — not a secretary, not a Pemex or CFE director — decides alone what stays classified. Only national security and open proceedings can be reserved, and even then in public versions. The old INAI cost over a billion pesos a year — and its portal "was down all the time." The decree goes to Congress in September to become law.
